name: Read the sales history
before_text: Read how many weekly sales values are known and how many are missing.
change: Reveal unresolved records. Do not alter the data.
observe: Read the missing or unresolved records. Missing means unknown, not zero.
questions: After revealing the record details, how many weekly sales values are still unknown? Did showing the details change the sales history?
A colleague suggests entering zero for every unknown week before preparing the sales estimate. What would zero tell the forecast that the records do not tell us?
Write two sentences to that colleague: what can you report from the history, and what should you ask them to check?
answers: Ten weekly sales values remain unknown. Revealing details changes what is displayed, not the data: 198 known values remain.
Zero would tell the forecast that no units were sold in those weeks. The records do not establish that; replacing unknowns with zero could pull an average down without evidence.
“We have 198 known weekly sales values and 10 unknown values. Please check the missing and unresolved source records before we treat those weeks as zero sales.”

name: Review a promotion assumption
before_text: Read the full-history promotion group means and fixed MA3 reference.
change: Assume a promotion next week and a 20% increase over the fixed reference.
observe: Compare reference and conditional scenario. Separate observations from the commercial assumption.
questions: When the assumed promotion increase changes from 0% to 20%, which SKU_A quantity changes, and which stays the same?
Sales proposes a promotion next week. Does the higher planning quantity mean we have already observed more sales, or that we are planning for a different situation? Use the two displayed quantities.
A colleague asks, “Why is next week’s plan higher than the original forecast?” Give a two-sentence explanation that names the assumption and one detail about the planned promotion to check.
answers: The conditional plan rises from 150.33 to 180.40 units. The original MA3 reference stays at 150.33 units.
We are planning for a different situation: an assumed promotion with 20% higher sales. The extra quantity is not a newly observed sale or a measured effect of that future promotion.

“The original estimate is 150.33 units; the plan is 180.40 because we assumed a 20% increase for next week’s promotion. Please confirm the promotion timing and whether it is comparable to earlier events.” Other relevant checks include the promotion type and whether earlier promotions already influence the reference.

name: Compare forecast windows
before_text: Inspect naïve and MA3 on the validation period, 11 Aug–27 Oct 2024.
change: Inspect MA6 on exactly the same validation dates. The chart shows all three fixed candidates.
observe: Read the error comparison and the separate final check below. The helper chooses the method; you interpret what happened.
questions: For SKU_A, compare the MA3 and MA6 validation MAE on the same 12 weeks. Which has the smaller average error?
A colleague says, “Using six weeks instead of three must give a better forecast because it uses more history.” Does this run support that claim? Refer to the two MAE values.
On the separate final eight weeks, MA3 has MAE 20.42 and the previous-week forecast has MAE 20.38. What would you tell the colleague about whether MA3 has shown an accuracy improvement?
answers: MA3 has the smaller validation MAE: 20.83 units/week, compared with 36.54 for MA6 on the same 12 weeks.
No. MA6 has the larger error here. A longer average smooths more history, but that does not automatically make its estimates closer to actual sales.

“MA3 was better in the validation comparison, but its final error of 20.42 is almost the same as the previous-week forecast’s 20.38. This final check does not show an accuracy improvement over that simple forecast.” The method was selected before this check; these results are not used to choose again.

name: Change the planning horizon
before_text: Read the fixed weekly reference for SKU_A. Start with one future week.
change: Extend the horizon to four consecutive weeks. Keep the weekly reference unchanged.
observe: Compare units per week with total units over the selected period.
questions: After changing the period from one week to four weeks, compare the weekly estimate and the total. Which changes?
A colleague sees the four-week total and says, “Sales are now expected to be four times higher each week.” What has the colleague confused?
The sales manager asks for an estimate covering the next four weeks. Write a short reply giving the total and the weekly-sales assumption behind it.
answers: The weekly reference remains 150.33 units/week. The total changes from 150.33 units for one week to 601.33 units for four weeks, using the unrounded reference.
The colleague has confused a total for four weeks with a quantity for one week. This run repeats the same weekly estimate; it does not increase the sales rate.

“Estimated sales over the next four weeks are 601.33 units, assuming the same weekly sales level of about 150.33 units.” This calculation repeats a weekly estimate; it is not a separately tested forecast of changing sales in each future week.

name: Review a forecast against actual sales
before_text: Keep the original 150.33 forecast and the assumed+20% forecast 180.40 fixed. Use hypothetical actual sales 150.
change: Change the hypothetical actual to 190. Do not alter either forecast.
observe: Compare the two absolute-error bars and the displayed signed errors.
questions: Compare the two runs with hypothetical actual sales of 150 and 190 units. Which forecast is closer in each run?
Why does the closer forecast change even though neither forecast was edited? Use the actual sales and the error bars.
After the 190-unit example, Sales says, “The promotion adjustment worked, so we should always add 20%.” How would you explain what these two examples show?
answers: At 150 actual units, the original forecast is closer: absolute errors are 0.33 versus 30.40 units. At 190, the adjusted forecast is closer: 9.60 versus 39.67 units.

The actual outcome changes from 150 to 190. The fixed original estimate of 150.33 is nearer 150, while the fixed adjusted estimate of 180.40 is nearer 190. The error bars measure distance from each outcome.

“The adjustment is closer in the 190-unit example, but the original is closer in the 150-unit example. These hypothetical outcomes show why we compare both estimates against actual sales; they do not establish that a promotion causes a 20% increase or that this adjustment always helps.”
